nodes.label: Behavioral Welfare Economics
nodes.description: How to evaluate welfare when individual choices may not reflect true preferences. The Bernheim-Rangel "beyond revealed preference" framework provides foundations for behavioral welfare economics without assuming choices are utility-maximizing.

nodes.label: Beyond Revealed Preference
key_concepts: Choice process data as auxiliary information

nodes.label: Corrective Taxation & Policy
nodes.description: Optimal design of taxes and regulations when agents have biases. Extends Pigouvian taxation to internalities — self-imposed harms from present bias, inattention, or misperceptions — in addition to externalities.

nodes.label: Distributional Concerns
key_concepts: Optimal soda tax with income heterogeneity

nodes.label: Nudges & Default Effects
nodes.description: Behavioral interventions that alter choice architecture without restricting options. Libertarian paternalism: preserve choice freedom while steering people toward better outcomes through defaults, framing, and social norms.

nodes.label: Sludge & Administrative Burden
nodes.description: Frictions in accessing public programs. Complexity, stigma, and psychological costs reduce take-up of beneficial programs, imposing welfare costs on eligible non-participants.

nodes.label: Present Bias & Self-Control
nodes.description: Time-inconsistent preferences and their policy implications. The β-δ quasi-hyperbolic discounting model captures present focus that distorts savings, health, and labor supply decisions.

nodes.label: Earnings & Labor Policy
nodes.description: Behavioral dimensions of income taxation, labor supply, and social insurance. Covers tax misperceptions, biased beliefs about unemployment, and behavioral hazard in health insurance.

nodes.label: Income Tax Misperceptions
key_concepts: Optimal income tax with behavioral agents

nodes.label: Empirical Methods
nodes.description: Methods for measuring biases and evaluating behavioral interventions in public economics contexts. Bridges structural and reduced-form traditions.

nodes.label: Beyond Revealed Preference: Choice-Theoretic Foundations for Behavioral Welfare Economics
nodes.summary: Proposes the Bernheim-Rangel framework for welfare analysis without relying on revealed preference. Introduces the unambiguous choice relation P* as the unique welfare criterion satisfying three basic properties. Foundation of modern behavioral welfare economics.

nodes.label: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly: A Unified Approach to Behavioral Welfare Economics
nodes.summary: Refines the Bernheim-Rangel framework. Distinguishes direct vs. indirect judgments, argues that behavioral economics challenges indirect but not direct judgments. Provides revised premises for choice-oriented welfare analysis.

nodes.label: Behavioral Economics and Public Policy: A Pragmatic Perspective
nodes.summary: Advocates for the sufficient statistics approach: use reduced-form estimates of behavioral wedges to evaluate policy without fully specifying cognitive models. Frames decision utility vs. experienced utility as alternative welfare foundations.

nodes.label: Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting
nodes.summary: Popularizes the β-δ (quasi-hyperbolic discounting) model. Shows that illiquid assets serve as commitment devices for present-biased consumers. Foundational paper for the self-control literature in behavioral economics.

nodes.label: Temptation and Self-Control
nodes.summary: Axiomatizes temptation preferences where consumers experience a penalty when choosing anything other than the most tempting option. Accounts for choice reversals without time inconsistency.

nodes.label: Evaluating Behaviorally-Motivated Policy: Experimental Evidence from the Lightbulb Market
nodes.summary: Within-subject experiment on lightbulb purchases. Debiasing intervention reveals consumer undervaluation of energy costs. Derives price-metric bias γ and computes optimal corrective subsidy using the internality framework.

nodes.label: Is Addiction 'Rational'? Theory and Evidence
nodes.summary: Incorporates quasi-hyperbolic discounting into the rational addiction model. Derives optimal cigarette tax that corrects both externalities and internalities from self-control failures. Key application of the modified Pigouvian principle.

nodes.label: Tax Incidence when Individuals are Time-Inconsistent: the Case of Cigarette Excise Taxes
nodes.summary: Shows that cigarette taxes can be welfare-improving even for low-income consumers when present bias is sufficiently severe and demand is elastic. Addresses the regressivity concern for sin taxes.

nodes.label: Regressive Sin Taxes, with an Application to the Optimal Soda Tax
nodes.summary: Estimates optimal soda tax accounting for both internalities and externalities. Develops framework for optimal tax when sin goods are regressively consumed. Finds moderate tax justified despite regressivity when corrective benefits dominate.

nodes.label: Optimal Sin Taxes
nodes.summary: Studies taxation of unhealthy foods under present-bias. Shows optimal tax is positive whenever present focus causes overconsumption and consumers are price-sensitive. General application of the modified Pigouvian principle.

nodes.label: Energy Policy with Externalities and Internalities
nodes.summary: Studies optimal policy mix (energy tax + appliance subsidy) when consumers underweight future energy costs. Key result: optimal energy tax is below the Pigouvian level because standard consumers over-respond to it.

nodes.label: Optimal Taxation with Behavioral Agents
nodes.summary: General framework for optimal taxation with behavioral agents. Derives formulas for both commodity and income taxes that generalize standard sufficient statistics by adding price-metric bias terms. Shows Ramsey-style formulas re-emerge with non-salient commodity taxes.

nodes.label: Addiction and Cue-triggered Decision Processes
nodes.summary: Models addiction as cue-triggered hot states. Argues welfare-relevant domain excludes choices made in triggered states using neurobiological evidence. Derives the surprising result that optimal tax on addictive goods may be negative.

nodes.label: Salience and Taxation: Theory and Evidence
nodes.summary: Field experiment + natural experiment showing consumers underreact to taxes not included in posted prices (σ ≈ 0.06–0.35). Derives efficiency cost formula showing underreaction reduces deadweight loss through two channels.

nodes.label: E-ZTAX: Tax Salience and Tax Rates
nodes.summary: Electronic toll collection (E-ZPass) reduces tax salience, leading governments to raise toll rates. Natural experiment showing that salience affects the political economy of taxation.

nodes.label: Libertarian Paternalism
nodes.summary: Introduces libertarian paternalism: preserving choice while steering people toward better outcomes through defaults and framing. Argues planners inevitably influence choices through defaults, so should do so in welfare-enhancing ways.

nodes.label: The Short-Run and Long-Run Effects of Behavioral Interventions: Experimental Evidence from Energy Conservation
nodes.summary: Evaluates Opower social comparison nudges for energy conservation. Finds effects persist but decay over time. Estimates welfare effects of the nudge using willingness-to-pay elicitation.

nodes.label: The Power of Suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) Participation and Savings Behavior
nodes.summary: Seminal paper documenting dramatic default effects in 401(k) enrollment. Auto- enrollment increases participation rates from ~49% to ~86%. First rigorous evidence of status quo bias in retirement savings.

nodes.label: Optimal Defaults and Active Decisions
nodes.summary: Derives optimal 401(k) default contribution rate. Under long-run welfare criterion, sufficiently low β justifies active choice requirements rather than passive defaults. Shows opt-out maximization can be welfare-improving.

nodes.label: The Welfare Economics of Default Options in 401(k) Plans
nodes.summary: Applies Bernheim-Rangel framework to 401(k) defaults. Shows EVA and EVB bounds on welfare effects lead to similar optimal defaults for contribution rates below 20%. Default is generally insensitive to the decision frame in this range.

nodes.label: Tying Odysseus to the Mast: Evidence from a Commitment Savings Product in the Philippines
nodes.summary: RCT of commitment savings account (SEED) in Philippines. Documents demand for commitment devices, particularly among present-biased individuals. Balance increased 82% relative to control group.

nodes.label: Poverty and Self-Control
nodes.summary: Formalizes internal self-control through history-dependent equilibria. Shows external commitments can undermine internal self-regulation. Low initial assets trap people in poverty by limiting self-control strategies.

nodes.label: Psychological Frictions and the Incomplete Take-Up of Social Benefits
nodes.summary: Field experiment on EITC take-up. Simplified notices dramatically increase take-up. Psychological frictions—not stigma—are the main barrier. Addresses the incomplete take-up puzzle for redistributive programs.

nodes.label: Taxpayer Confusion: Evidence from the Child Tax Credit
nodes.summary: RD design showing taxpayers confuse lump-sum transfers with marginal tax changes. Loss of CTC associated with decline in reported wage income, even though CTC is lump-sum and should not affect labor supply incentives.

nodes.label: Behavioral Hazard in Health Insurance
nodes.summary: Derives optimal copay formula for health insurance with behavioral consumers. Biases can cause over-use of some medications and under-use of others. Extends behavioral public economics framework to health insurance design.

nodes.label: Unemployed but Optimistic: Optimal Insurance Design with Biased Beliefs
nodes.summary: Modifies Baily-Chetty optimal unemployment insurance formula for biased beliefs about reemployment prospects. Slope effect (return to search) vs. level effect (job-finding probability) have different policy implications.

nodes.label: Do Pharmacists Buy Bayer? Informed Shoppers and the Brand Premium
nodes.summary: Pharmacists and doctors buy generic drugs more than laypeople. Uses expert choices as rational consumer benchmark to measure bias from imperfect information. Application of the rational consumer benchmark welfare method.

nodes.label: A Method for Evaluating the Quality of Financial Decision Making
nodes.summary: Introduces financial competence measure based on WTA discrepancies for equivalent claims. Shows standard financial education increases tested knowledge but not decision quality—motivational rhetoric drives behavioral change, not substance.

nodes.label: Ramsey Strikes Back: Optimal Commodity Taxes and Redistribution in the Presence of Salience Effects
nodes.summary: Shows Atkinson-Stiglitz theorem breaks down with non-salient commodity taxes. Optimal commodity taxes follow Diamond (1975) Many-person Ramsey rule. Differential commodity taxes become useful even when income taxation is available.
